blocks.html: In 1922 an archaeologist named Howard Carter stepped down a dark staircase in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, held up a candle and peered through a hole into a sealed tomb. Someone asked if he could see anything. "Yes," he answered, "wonderful things." It was the tomb of the boy king Tutankhamun, untouched for more than 3,000 years.

History is the true story of people in the past. We learn it from sources. A primary source comes from the time itself: a letter, a diary, a coin, a tool, a photograph. A secondary source is written later by someone studying the past, like this lesson or a history book.

blocks.name: histstory-pic

items: A clay pot
A coin
A letter
Bones
A statue
An old photo

blocks.cap: Things people left behind are clues. Each one is a primary source.

blocks.html: Archaeologists dig carefully for things people left behind, from tiny beads to whole cities. They write down exactly where each thing was found, because the layer of soil tells its age: deeper layers are usually older. Historians read old writings, compare them and ask questions: Who wrote this? When? Why? Did they see it themselves?

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A source is made by someone in the past and studied by someone today.

blocks.title: Primary or secondary?
blocks.q: Which of these is a primary source about the Roman city of Pompeii: a coin found in the ruins of Pompeii, or a children's book about Pompeii written in 2015?
steps: The coin was made and used in Pompeii itself, before the city was buried in AD 79.
The book was written almost 2,000 years later by someone studying the city.
blocks.a: The coin is a primary source. The book is a secondary source.

blocks.html: Thinking one source tells the whole truth. Two people can see the same event differently. Historians compare several sources before they decide what happened.

Some of the best clues were found by accident. In 1799 French soldiers digging in Egypt found the Rosetta Stone. It had the same message in three scripts, and it helped scholars read Egyptian hieroglyphs for the first time in more than a thousand years.

items: Be a family historian. Ask a grandparent or older relative three questions: Where did you grow up? What did you do for fun as a child? What has changed most since then?
Write down the answers. You just made a primary source: an interview!
Find one old object at home, such as a photo, a letter or a coin. What can it tell you about the past?

blocks.html: Going further. See how the Rosetta Stone was found and read on the Timeline and in Ancient Egypt for Young Explorers. Older students learn to read sources closely in Primary and Secondary Sources (U.S. History I).

How do we number the years? Long ago, every land counted its own way: from the founding of a city, or from the year a king began to rule. About AD 525, a monk named Dionysius Exiguus worked out a count starting from the birth of Jesus. In time, much of the world came to use it.

Years after the birth of Jesus are marked AD (from the Latin anno Domini, "in the year of the Lord") and counted forward: AD 1, AD 2, AD 3… Years before are marked BC ("before Christ") and counted backward: 3 BC, 2 BC, 1 BC. There is no year 0: 1 BC is followed right away by AD 1.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: BC years count down toward the start; AD years count up. The year after 1 BC is AD 1.

blocks.html: So with BC dates, a bigger number is longer ago. Rome was founded (in legend) in 753 BC, and the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC, 23 years earlier.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: A time line puts events in order, from earlier to later.

head: To find years between…
Do this
Example
rows: a BC date and an AD date

blocks.title: How long apart?
blocks.q: Julius Caesar died in 44 BC. The emperor Augustus died in AD 14. How many years apart were they?
steps: One date is BC and one is AD, so add: 44 + 14 = 58.
There is no year 0 between 1 BC and AD 1, so take away 1: 58 − 1 = 57.
blocks.a: 57 years.

blocks.html: A century is 100 years. The years 1801 to 1900 are the 19th century, because they finish the 19th group of a hundred years. We live in the 21st century: the 2000s.
Reading 500 BC as later than 300 BC because 500 is the bigger number. With BC dates, bigger means earlier.
You may also see BCE and CE ("before the Common Era" and "Common Era"). They use the same numbers; only the letters are different. This course writes BC and AD.

items: Make a time line of your own life on a long strip of paper: one hand-width for each year.
Mark the year you were born, when you learned to walk, your first day of school, and other big moments.
Then make a family time line: add the years your parents and grandparents were born.

blocks.html: Going further. Explore the Timeline of the Ancient World, from the pyramids to the fall of Rome. Older students practice with dates and periods in Dates and Periods.

Picture a family long ago, walking through the hills with everything they own on their backs. They follow the herds of deer and gather nuts, seeds and berries as the seasons change. For most of the human story, this is how people lived: as hunter-gatherers.

About 12,000 years ago, people in the hills of the Middle East, in a curve of land called the Fertile Crescent, began to plant seeds of wild wheat and barley and to tame sheep, goats and cattle. This change, from gathering food to growing it, is called the Agricultural Revolution.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: An early farmer with a sickle, a curved blade for cutting grain.

blocks.html: Farming changed everything. Farmers had to stay near their fields, so they built houses and villages. A field could feed more people than the wild land, so the number of people grew. Extra food could be stored, so not everyone had to farm: some people became potters, weavers and toolmakers.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Some of the oldest farming villages grew in the Fertile Crescent, near rivers. Jericho and Çatalhöyük are among the oldest towns we know.

blocks.html: Farming began on its own in other places too: rice and millet in China, corn, beans and squash in Mexico, and potatoes in the Andes mountains of South America.

head: Hunter-gatherers
Farmers
rows: stored grain in pots and bins

blocks.title: Why stay?
blocks.q: Why did farming families build lasting houses, when hunter-gatherers did not?
steps: Crops take months to grow, and fields need care.
Farmers had to stay near their fields to plant, weed, guard and harvest them.
blocks.a: Because they had to stay near their fields all year.

blocks.html: Picturing early people living alongside dinosaurs. The last big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, long before the first people.

items: Plant a dry bean in a cup of damp soil on a sunny windowsill. Keep the soil damp, not soaking.
Measure and draw it every few days. How long until it sprouts? Early farmers had to wait and watch like this.
Look in your kitchen for foods first grown by early farmers: wheat (bread), rice, corn, beans and potatoes.

blocks.html: Going further. The Three Sisters lesson (Young Learners) tells how corn, beans and squash were grown together in North America. Older students see farming and food today in Human Geography.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: More than 5,000 years ago, in the land between two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, a scribe sat with a lump of wet clay and a reed pen cut to a sharp wedge. Press, press, press: he was writing down how many sheep a farmer owed the temple. He was using one of the first kinds of writing in the world.

Mesopotamia means "the land between the rivers," in today's Iraq. There the Sumerians built the first cities, such as Ur and Uruk, about 3500 BC. They invented cuneiform writing (wedge-shaped marks in clay) about 3200 BC and were among the first people to use the wheel.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Sumer's cities lay near the Tigris and Euphrates, in today's Iraq.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A scribe with a clay tablet. Scribes went to school for years to learn hundreds of signs.

blocks.html: Each city had a giant stepped temple called a ziggurat, and farmers dug canals to bring river water to their fields. Sumerians counted in sixties, and that is why we still have 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.

About 1754 BC, Hammurabi, king of Babylon, had nearly 300 laws carved on a tall stone so that people could know the rules. Some laws seem very harsh to us, like "an eye for an eye." The big idea was new: the laws were written down for all to see, and the same rules applied each time.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: Mesopotamia on a time line.

blocks.title: How long ago?
blocks.q: Hammurabi's laws were carved about 1754 BC. About how many years before AD 2000 is that?
steps: One date is BC and one is AD: add them: 1,754 + 2,000 = 3,754.
Take away 1 for the missing year 0: 3,753.
blocks.a: About 3,750 years.

blocks.html: Thinking the first writing used letters like ours. Cuneiform used hundreds of signs, and it began as a way to keep count of grain, animals and other goods.

items: Flatten a ball of play dough or modeling clay into a tablet.
Use the end of a craft stick or a pencil to press wedge-shaped marks into it. Make up a sign for "sheep" and count five sheep.
Hold up your tablet: could someone else read it? That is why scribes had to agree on the signs.

blocks.html: Going further. See the Royal Game of Ur on the Timeline, one of the oldest board games known. For more about early writing systems, the Ancient Scripts Ladder is for older students.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: Every summer, the Nile River rose and spread over its banks. When the water went down, it left a layer of thick black mud on the fields. Farmers planted in it and grew wheat, barley and flax. The Greek writer Herodotus called Egypt "the gift of the river."

Ancient Egypt grew up along the Nile. About 3100 BC, a king joined Upper and Lower Egypt into one kingdom. Kings called pharaohs ruled for about 3,000 years. Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs, built pyramids as tombs for their kings and preserved the dead as mummies.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Almost all Egyptians lived close to the Nile. Beyond it lay desert.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A pharaoh in a striped headcloth, a scribe and a farmer.

blocks.html: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 2560 BC. It was the tallest building in the world for almost 4,000 years. Workers moved more than two million stone blocks with copper tools, wooden sledges, ramps and a great deal of teamwork.

Egyptians believed in many gods and in a life after death. They hoped a person's spirit would live on, so they preserved bodies and filled tombs with things for the next life. Those tombs are a treasure for archaeologists today.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: Three thousand years of pharaohs.

blocks.title: Closer in time
blocks.q: Cleopatra died in 30 BC. The Great Pyramid was built about 2560 BC. Was Cleopatra closer in time to the pyramid builders or to us (AD 2000)?
steps: Cleopatra to the pyramid: 2,560 − 30 = 2,530 years.
Cleopatra to AD 2000: 30 + 2,000 − 1 = 2,029 years.
blocks.a: Closer to us! The pyramid was already ancient in her day.

blocks.html: Thinking all the famous Egyptians lived at about the same time. Egypt's history is so long that the Great Pyramid was older to Cleopatra than Cleopatra is to us.

items: Write your name in hieroglyphs, using sound signs, with the Egyptology course's cartouche lesson.
Make a small pyramid from sugar cubes or building blocks. How many blocks does each layer need?

blocks.html: Going further. A whole course for young readers: Ancient Egypt for Young Explorers (try Your Name in a Cartouche). See the Great Pyramid and Hatshepsut on the Timeline, and read about Herodotus on the young readers' path of Herodotus: The Histories.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: About 4,500 years ago, on the banks of the Indus River in today's Pakistan and northwest India, people built cities that look surprisingly modern. Streets ran straight, in a grid. Houses were made of baked bricks of the same size, and many had a bathroom with a drain that ran into covered sewers under the street.

The Indus Valley civilization, with cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, was at its height about 2600 to 1900 BC. Its people traded with Mesopotamia and carved small stone seals with animals and signs. Nobody has yet learned to read their writing.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: The Indus cities, and Varanasi on the Ganges, one of the oldest cities still lived in today.

blocks.html: Later, kingdoms grew along the Ganges River. About 2,300 years ago the Maurya family united much of India. Its most famous emperor, Ashoka, won a terrible war, and the suffering he saw changed him. He became a follower of the Buddha and had messages carved on stone pillars across his empire, asking people to be kind, honest and respectful of other faiths.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: Ancient India.

blocks.html: Scholars in ancient India also gave the world a great gift: the numerals we use, with a zero and place value. In AD 628 the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero.

blocks.title: Read the clues
blocks.q: The Indus script cannot be read. How do we know Indus cities were planned?
steps: Archaeologists dug up the cities and mapped them.
They found straight streets in a grid, same-size bricks and covered drains in many neighborhoods.
blocks.a: From the cities themselves: the ruins show careful planning.

blocks.html: Thinking we can read every ancient writing. The Indus script and some others are still a mystery, waiting for a new Rosetta Stone.

items: On graph paper, plan a city like Mohenjo-daro: main streets running north–south and east–west, blocks of houses, a well, and drains that lead out of the city.
Where would you put the big public bath and the granary (grain store)?

blocks.html: Going further. Find India and its rivers in Asia: Mountains, Rivers and Deserts (World Geography). Our numerals and zero are the start of the Math Ladder.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: About 3,200 years ago, priests of the Shang kings in China scratched questions on turtle shells and the shoulder bones of cattle: "Will it rain?" "Will the harvest be good?" Then they heated the bones until they cracked and read the cracks as answers. These oracle bones hold the oldest Chinese writing we know, and many of their signs are the great-grandparents of Chinese characters used today.

China's history is counted in dynasties: ruling families that passed power from parent to child. The Shang (about 1600 to 1046 BC) wrote on bones; Confucius (551 to 479 BC) taught about respect and good government; the Qin united China in 221 BC; the Han (206 BC to AD 220) traded silk along the Silk Road and made paper.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Chinese civilization grew along the Yellow River.

blocks.html: Confucius was a teacher. He taught that children should honor their parents, that rulers should be fair and set a good example, and that people should keep learning all their lives. His sayings were collected by his students in a book called the Analects, and his ideas shaped China for more than 2,000 years.

In 221 BC, the king of Qin defeated the other kingdoms and called himself the First Emperor. He made everyone use the same writing, money and weights, and he joined older walls into a long wall in the north. He was buried with an army of about 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, the Terracotta Army, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

blocks.name: histstory-pic

items: Oracle bones
The Great Wall
Clay soldiers
Silk
Paper

blocks.cap: Ancient China gave the world silk, paper and much more.

blocks.title: Which dynasty?
blocks.q: A Chinese family in about AD 105 is using a new kind of writing sheet made from bark, hemp and rags. Which dynasty is ruling?
steps: The Han ruled from 206 BC to AD 220.
AD 105 falls inside that time.
blocks.a: The Han dynasty. (Tradition says an official named Cai Lun improved paper in AD 105.)

blocks.html: Thinking the Great Wall was built all at once. It was built, joined and rebuilt over about 2,000 years; most of what visitors walk on today was built by the Ming dynasty, after AD 1368.

items: Dip a clean paintbrush in water and paint the Chinese character for "person," 人, on a dry sidewalk or a chalkboard. It looks like a person walking.
Find something made of silk or paper at home. Both were first made in China.

blocks.html: Going further. See China and its great rivers in Asia: Mountains, Rivers and Deserts. This course comes back to China in Inventions of China and the Samurai of Japan.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: Ancient Greece was not one country. It was hundreds of city-states: each a city with its own farms around it, its own laws and its own army. They shared a language, gods and the Olympic Games, first held in 776 BC, when wars stopped so athletes could travel safely to Olympia.

In Athens, from about 508 BC, citizens met on a hillside and voted on laws themselves: a democracy, "rule by the people." Sparta was ruled by two kings and a council, and every boy trained to be a soldier from the age of seven. Athens loved art, plays and learning; Sparta prized discipline and courage.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Athens, Sparta and Olympia, with the Persian Empire to the east.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Two ways of life: an Athenian citizen with a scroll, and a soldier with a shield.

blocks.html: In 490 BC the mighty Persian Empire invaded Greece. The Athenians won a surprise victory at Marathon. Ten years later the Persians came back. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, King Leonidas and his Spartans held them off for three days, and then the Athenian navy beat the Persian fleet at Salamis. Greece stayed free.

blocks.title: Who voted?
blocks.q: Could every person living in Athens vote in the assembly?
steps: Only free men whose parents were Athenian citizens could vote.
Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in Athens could not.
blocks.a: No, only male citizens. Still, it was a bold new idea: ordinary citizens deciding together.

blocks.html: Thinking Athens and Sparta were always friends. They fought together against Persia, then fought each other in the long Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BC).

items: Hold a family assembly, Athenian style. Choose a question (What should we have for dinner on Friday?), let everyone speak, then vote with a show of hands.
Hold mini Olympic Games in the yard: a running race, a long jump and a throwing contest with a soft ball. The winners get a crown of leaves, as at Olympia.

blocks.html: Going further. Read the stories of Solon, Leonidas and Pericles in Famous Men of Greece. Play Thermopylae. See Marathon and Thermopylae and Salamis on the Timeline, and the young readers' path of Herodotus: The Histories, who told the story of the Persian Wars.

sources.name: John H. Haaren and A. B. Poland, Famous Men of Greece (1904), public domain
Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: In the marketplace of Athens, an old man in a plain cloak stopped people and asked them questions. "What is courage?" "What is justice?" Whatever they answered, he asked another question, until they saw they did not know as much as they thought. His name was Socrates, and he said that wisdom begins with knowing what you don't know.
Three great Greek thinkers were teacher and student: Socrates taught Plato, Plato taught Aristotle, and Aristotle taught a prince named Alexander. They are called philosophers, "lovers of wisdom."

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Teacher and student: Socrates → Plato → Aristotle → Alexander.

blocks.html: Socrates wrote nothing down; we know him from Plato's books. Plato started a school in Athens called the Academy. Aristotle studied animals, plants, the stars, poetry and government, and wrote books on all of them. Another Greek, Archimedes of Syracuse, worked out how levers and floating things work.

Alexander the Great became king of Macedonia at 20, in 336 BC. In just over ten years he conquered the Persian Empire and marched as far as India. He founded cities named Alexandria; the one in Egypt became a great center of learning with a famous library. He died at 32, and his empire split among his generals, but Greek language and ideas spread across the lands he had crossed.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Alexander's march, roughly, from Macedonia to Egypt, Persia and the Indus.

blocks.title: Who taught whom?
blocks.q: Who was Aristotle's teacher, and who was his most famous student?
steps: The chain goes Socrates → Plato → Aristotle → Alexander.
The one before Aristotle is Plato; the one after is Alexander.
blocks.a: Plato taught him; Alexander was his student.

blocks.html: Mixing up the three philosophers. Remember the order, which is also alphabetical except for the first: S, P, A… then Alexander.

items: Play Socrates. Ask a family member, "What makes someone a good friend?" To each answer, ask a new "why" or "what about" question.
Afterward, write down the best answer you found together. Did the questions help you think more clearly?

blocks.html: Going further. The young readers' paths of The Trial of Socrates and Archimedes: The Works. See Alexander the Great and the Library of Alexandria on the Timeline, and read Famous Men of Greece.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: An old Roman story says twin baby boys, Romulus and Remus, were left by a river and cared for by a she-wolf. When they grew up, Romulus founded a city on seven hills by the Tiber River and named it after himself: Rome. The Romans dated their city from 753 BC.

At first kings ruled Rome. In 509 BC the Romans sent away their last king and made a republic: citizens elected leaders, two consuls who served for one year, and a council of experienced men called the Senate gave advice. The idea was that no one person should hold power for long.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A senator in a toga with a purple stripe, and a farmer. Early Romans were mostly farmers.

blocks.html: Over 250 years, Rome took over all of Italy. Then it fought three long wars with Carthage, a trading city in North Africa. In 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army with war elephants over the snowy Alps into Italy. Rome lost battle after battle but would not give up, and in the end it won.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Rome and Carthage, and Hannibal's march from Spain over the Alps.

blocks.html: A story Romans loved: in 458 BC, enemies trapped a Roman army. The Senate sent for Cincinnatus, who was plowing his small farm. He was made dictator, beat the enemy in about two weeks, then gave up his power and went home to his plow. Romans, and later Americans like George Washington, admired him for giving up power.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: The Roman Republic.

blocks.title: Republic or democracy?
blocks.q: In Athens, citizens voted on each law themselves. In Rome, citizens elected consuls and other leaders who governed for them. Which was the republic?
steps: In a republic, people elect leaders to make decisions for them.
That was Rome.
blocks.a: Rome was the republic; Athens was a direct democracy.

blocks.html: Thinking a republic means everyone is equal. In Rome, rich families had much more power than poor ones, and enslaved people had no say at all.

items: Hold a family election: nominate two "consuls" for a week who decide the games after dinner. Why might Rome have chosen two, and only for a year?
Find the Latin words on a U.S. coin or dollar bill, such as E pluribus unum, "out of many, one."

blocks.html: Going further. Read about Romulus, Cincinnatus and Hannibal in Famous Men of Rome. See the republic begins and Hannibal crosses the Alps on the Timeline, and the young readers' path of Plutarch: Roman Lives.

sources.name: John H. Haaren and A. B. Poland, Famous Men of Rome (1904), public domain
Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: By 49 BC, the general Julius Caesar had conquered Gaul (today's France) and was the most powerful man in Rome. He made himself dictator for life. Some senators feared he would end the republic, and on the Ides of March (March 15), 44 BC, they killed him. Years of war followed.

In 27 BC Caesar's adopted son Octavian took the name Augustus and became the first Roman emperor. The Roman Empire stretched around the whole Mediterranean Sea. For about 200 years, a time called the Pax Romana ("Roman peace"), most of the empire was at peace.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: A few cities of the Roman Empire at its height, from Britain to Egypt.

blocks.html: Romans were great builders. They made about 50,000 miles of paved roads, so that "all roads lead to Rome." Aqueducts carried fresh water from the hills into cities, sloping gently downhill the whole way. They built arches, domes and the Colosseum, where 50,000 people watched games, using a strong Roman concrete.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Roman citizens wore the toga on special days.

blocks.html: In AD 79 the volcano Vesuvius erupted and buried the town of Pompeii in ash. Digging there since the 1700s has shown us Roman houses, shops, bakeries and even writing scratched on walls.

blocks.title: First emperor
blocks.q: Was Julius Caesar the first Roman emperor?
steps: Caesar ruled as dictator and was killed in 44 BC.
Augustus, his adopted son, became the first emperor in 27 BC.
blocks.a: No. Augustus was the first emperor.

blocks.html: Thinking Romans spoke Italian. They spoke Latin. Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian grew out of it, and more than half of English words come from Latin, many of them through French.

items: Build an arch from a row of sugar cubes, small blocks or folded cardboard. Lean the pieces together over a curved support, then take the support away. Does it stand?
Write today's date in Roman numerals: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1,000.

blocks.html: Going further. Play Aqueduct Switches and Charioteer. See the Ides of March and Augustus on the Timeline; read Famous Men of Rome and the young readers' path of Virgil: The Aeneid.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: All through history, people have asked big questions: Who made the world? How should we live? What happens after we die? The answers of the world's faiths have shaped laws, holidays, art and the way billions of people live today. In this lesson we describe what the followers of three ancient faiths believe, in the way they themselves would describe it.

Judaism: Jews worship one God, who they believe made a covenant (a solemn promise) with Abraham and gave the law to Moses. Hinduism: Hindus follow ancient teachings from India, the Vedas, and many honor God in many forms. Buddhism: Buddhists follow the teachings of the Buddha, who taught a path to end suffering.

head: Faith
Began
Holy writings
Some beliefs; a festival
rows: land of Israel, over 3,000 years ago
the Hebrew Bible, beginning with the Torah
one God, the Ten Commandments, the Sabbath; Passover
the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita
the Buddha's teachings, collected by his followers
the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path; Vesak

blocks.html: The Jewish scriptures tell how God called Abraham to a new land, and how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. Jews trace their history through kings like David and Solomon, who built a temple in Jerusalem. Judaism's belief in one God was shared by Christianity and Islam, which began later.

Siddhartha Gautama was a prince in northern India, born at Lumbini in today's Nepal. Buddhist tradition says he left his palace after seeing sickness, old age and death, and searched for years for the cause of suffering. Sitting under a tree, he reached what Buddhists call enlightenment, and was called the Buddha, "the awakened one." He taught for about 45 years.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Where these faiths began. Today their followers live all over the world.

blocks.title: Whose belief?
blocks.q: A friend tells you about Diwali, when families light lamps to celebrate the victory of light over darkness. Which faith's festival is she describing?
steps: Diwali, the festival of lights, is a Hindu festival.
(Sikhs and Jains keep their own celebrations at the same time of year.)
blocks.a: Hinduism.

blocks.html: Speaking about another person's faith as if it were just a story. We say "Hindus believe…" or "Jews celebrate…" and listen with respect, as we would want others to do for us.

items: Look at a calendar that lists holidays of several faiths. Which ones fall this month?
If you know a family of another faith, ask them politely about a holiday they keep and what it means to them.

blocks.html: Going further. India's land and rivers in Asia: Mountains, Rivers and Deserts. Older students meet ancient Egyptian beliefs in Many Gods (Young Explorers).

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: About 2,000 years ago, in Judea, a land ruled by the Roman Empire, a Jewish teacher from the town of Nazareth traveled with a small band of followers. His name was Jesus. He taught in villages and on hillsides, told stories called parables, and spoke of loving God and loving your neighbor.

Christians believe that Jesus is the Son of God, that he died on a cross for the sins of the world, and that he rose from the dead three days later. His followers wrote about his life and teaching in the four Gospels, which with other early writings make up the New Testament of the Christian Bible.

After Jesus's death, about AD 30, his followers, the apostles, began to spread his teaching. Paul traveled thousands of miles around the Mediterranean, starting Christian communities and writing them letters. The good Roman roads and the shared Greek language helped the message travel.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Christianity spread from Jerusalem along the roads and sea routes of the Roman Empire.

blocks.html: For almost 300 years, Christians were often mistreated in the Roman Empire, because they would not worship the emperor or the Roman gods. Then, in AD 313, the emperor Constantine allowed Christians to worship freely. In AD 380, Christianity became the official religion of the empire.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline

events: Dionysius counts years from Jesus's birth

blocks.cap: The early centuries of Christianity.

blocks.title: Why AD?
blocks.q: Why do the years go from BC to AD around the time of Jesus?
steps: About AD 525 the monk Dionysius Exiguus counted the years from the birth of Jesus, as he worked it out.
His count spread across Europe and later the world.
blocks.a: Because the count was set up to start from the birth of Jesus.

blocks.html: Thinking people at the time of Jesus wrote dates in AD. That count was worked out about 500 years later. (Most historians today think Dionysius was a few years off, and that Jesus was born a few years "BC.")

items: Read the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) together, or the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), and talk about what it teaches.
Find Jerusalem, Rome and the Mediterranean Sea on a globe or a map.

blocks.html: Going further. See the ministry of Jesus and the New Testament on the Timeline. Older students read Augustine on the young readers' path of Augustine: Confessions.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: By AD 400, the Roman Empire was too big to rule from one place. It had been split into a western half, ruled from Rome and later Ravenna, and an eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, a city the emperor Constantine had built on the Bosporus strait where Europe meets Asia.

The Western Roman Empire grew weak: armies fought over who would be emperor, taxes were heavy, and Germanic peoples moved across the borders. In AD 410 the Visigoths captured Rome, and in AD 476 the last western emperor, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was removed from the throne. The eastern half lived on for almost 1,000 years more as the Byzantine Empire, until AD 1453.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: The empire split into West (around Rome) and East (around Constantinople).

blocks.html: The greatest Byzantine emperor, Justinian (ruled AD 527 to 565), collected all the Roman laws into one great book. Many countries' laws still build on it. He also built the church of Hagia Sophia, "Holy Wisdom," whose huge dome seemed to float on light. Byzantine artists made glittering pictures from tiny pieces of colored glass and stone: mosaics.

blocks.name: histstory-pic

items: Hagia Sophia
Justinian's laws
Mosaics
Gold coins
Trade ships

blocks.cap: Byzantium kept Roman law and Greek learning alive.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: From one empire to two, and the long life of Byzantium.

blocks.title: How long did Byzantium last after the West fell?
blocks.q: The Western Empire ended in AD 476. Constantinople fell in AD 1453. How many years later was that?
steps: Both dates are AD, so subtract.
blocks.a: 977 years, almost 1,000.

blocks.html: Thinking all of the Roman Empire fell in 476. The eastern half, Byzantium, kept going. Its people still called themselves Romans.

items: Make a paper mosaic: cut colored paper into small squares and glue them onto card to make a picture or pattern, leaving tiny gaps between pieces.

blocks.html: Going further. See the last western emperor and Rome sacked on the Timeline. Play Mosaic Match. Read Famous Men of the Middle Ages (Alaric, Justinian and more).

John H. Haaren and A. B. Poland, Famous Men of the Middle Ages (1904), public domain
Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: In the trading city of Mecca, in Arabia, a merchant named Muhammad often went to a cave in the mountains to pray and think. Muslims believe that one night, about AD 610, the angel Gabriel came to him with a message from God, and that more messages came over the next 23 years.

Muslims, the followers of Islam, believe there is one God (in Arabic, Allah) and that Muhammad was God's final prophet. The messages he received were gathered into the Quran, the holy book of Islam. In AD 622 Muhammad and his followers moved to Medina; this journey, the Hijra, is the first year of the Islamic calendar.

Muslims follow the Five Pillars: declaring their faith, praying five times a day, giving to the poor, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and, if they can, making the pilgrimage to Mecca once in their lives. Within 100 years after Muhammad's death in AD 632, Muslim rulers governed lands from Spain to India.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Mecca and Medina, and two great centers of learning: Baghdad and Córdoba.

blocks.html: In Baghdad, in the 800s, scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and added discoveries of their own. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations; its title gave us the word algebra. Ibn al-Haytham did experiments on light and how we see. Doctors ran hospitals, and astronomers built observatories.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Scholars, merchants and translators made the cities of the Islamic world centers of learning and trade.

blocks.title: Where did our numbers come from?
blocks.q: We write numbers with ten digits, 0 to 9. Where did they come from?
steps: These numerals, with zero and place value, were developed in India.
Scholars in Baghdad, like al-Khwarizmi, wrote about them in Arabic, and Europeans learned them from Arabic books.
blocks.a: From India, by way of the Arab world: we call them Hindu-Arabic numerals.

blocks.html: Thinking the numerals 0 to 9 came from Rome. Romans used letters (I, V, X), and had no zero.

items: Draw an eight-pointed star pattern: trace around a round lid, mark eight evenly spaced points, and join them with a ruler. Patterns like this decorate many mosques and palaces.
Count in Roman numerals and in our numerals. Which is easier for adding big numbers?

blocks.html: Going further. The Math Ladder begins with place value, the idea that came to us through these scholars. The kingdoms of Africa that traded with the Islamic world come next in Kingdoms of Africa.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: On Christmas Day in the year AD 800, in Rome, the pope placed a crown on the head of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, and named him emperor. Charlemagne ruled much of Western Europe. He could read but found writing hard, yet he gathered scholars at his court and asked monasteries to start schools.

The Middle Ages are the 1,000 years between ancient times and modern times, about AD 500 to 1500. In Europe, kings gave land to lords; lords gave land to knights, who fought for them; and peasants farmed the land and gave a share of the crops. This system is called feudalism.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: People of a medieval kingdom. Most people were peasants.

blocks.html: Lords built castles of stone, with thick walls, towers and moats, to defend their lands. Knights trained from boyhood, first as pages and then as squires. They were expected to follow a code called chivalry: to be brave and loyal, and to protect the weak.

In monasteries, monks and nuns prayed, cared for the sick and travelers, and copied books by hand. A single Bible could take years to copy, and they decorated the pages with gold and bright colors. Without these copyists, many ancient books would have been lost.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: The Middle Ages in Europe.

blocks.html: In 1215, English barons made King John agree to the Magna Carta, "the great charter." It said that even the king had to obey the law. Then, from 1347, a terrible sickness called the Black Death spread across Europe and killed about one person in three.

blocks.title: Middle of what?
blocks.q: Why are they called the "Middle" Ages?
steps: Writers in the 1400s and 1500s thought of their own time as new, and of Greece and Rome as the ancient past.
The years in between they called the middle age.
blocks.a: They come between ancient times and modern times.

blocks.html: Thinking most people in the Middle Ages were knights or lived in castles. Nine out of ten people were peasants who farmed.

items: Design a coat of arms for your family on a shield shape: choose two colors and a picture that stands for something you value.
Write the first letter of your name large and decorate it with vines and gold (yellow) like a monk's illuminated page.

blocks.html: Going further. Famous Men of the Middle Ages tells the stories of Charlemagne, Alfred the Great and William the Conqueror. Play Nine Men's Morris, a game medieval people loved. The young readers' path of Chaucer: The Canterbury Tales meets medieval pilgrims.

sources.name: John H. Haaren and A. B. Poland, Famous Men of the Middle Ages (1904), public domain

blocks.html: In AD 793, monks on the little island of Lindisfarne, off the coast of England, saw strange ships with dragon-head prows coming in from the sea. The raiders took the monastery's treasures. For the next 250 years, people around Europe feared the arrival of the Vikings.

The Vikings came from Scandinavia: today's Norway, Denmark and Sweden. They sailed fast, shallow longships that could cross the ocean and also row up rivers. Some Vikings raided, but many more were farmers, traders and settlers. They settled in Britain, Ireland and France, and founded towns like Dublin.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Viking journeys: west to Iceland, Greenland and North America, and east down the rivers to Constantinople.

blocks.html: Vikings sailed west to settle Iceland (about AD 874) and Greenland. About AD 1000 Leif Erikson reached North America, which the Vikings called Vinland. Archaeologists found the remains of a Viking camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, in 1960. Other Vikings rowed east along the rivers of Russia to trade with Constantinople and Baghdad.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A Viking sailor with an oar.

blocks.html: Vikings told long stories called sagas, and Iceland kept many of them. In Iceland they also held one of the oldest parliaments in the world, the Althing, first held in AD 930.

blocks.title: Who came first?
blocks.q: Leif Erikson reached North America about AD 1000. Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492. How many years apart is that?
steps: Both dates are AD: subtract.
blocks.a: About 490 years.

blocks.html: Picturing Vikings in horned helmets. No Viking helmet with horns has ever been found. The horns come from costumes for an opera in the 1870s.

items: Fold a paper boat and float it in a sink or tub. Add coins one at a time. How many can it carry before it sinks?
Then try a wider, flatter boat. Longships were long, narrow and shallow, built for speed and for rivers.

blocks.html: Going further. Leif Erikson and other explorers in Explorers (Young Learners). Famous Men of the Middle Ages tells of Rollo the Viking.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: In AD 868, a man named Wang Jie paid to have a Buddhist book printed in honor of his parents. Printers carved each page, backward, on a block of wood, inked it and pressed paper onto it. A copy of that book, the Diamond Sutra, was found in a cave in western China in 1900. It is the oldest printed book with a date that we know of.

Under the Tang (AD 618 to 907) and Song (AD 960 to 1279) dynasties, China was one of the richest and most inventive lands on Earth. The Chinese invented or improved woodblock printing, gunpowder, the magnetic compass for ships and paper money.

blocks.name: histstory-pic

items: Woodblock printing
The compass
Paper money
Gunpowder (first used for fireworks)
Tea and porcelain

blocks.cap: Some of the inventions and trade goods of medieval China.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: China and Japan.

blocks.html: In Japan, an emperor reigned from the palace in Kyoto. From 1192, real power belonged to a military leader called the shogun, with warriors called samurai who served the great lords. Samurai followed a code of loyalty and self-control, and many also studied poetry, calligraphy and the tea ceremony.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: People of medieval Japan and China.

blocks.html: About AD 1000, a lady of the Japanese court, Murasaki Shikibu, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel. Later, in 1271, a young Italian merchant named Marco Polo set out for China. He stayed about 17 years, and his book amazed Europeans with stories of paper money and cities larger than any in Europe.

blocks.title: Printing before Gutenberg
blocks.q: The Diamond Sutra was printed in AD 868. Gutenberg printed his Bible about 1455. How many years earlier was the Diamond Sutra?
steps: Both dates are AD: subtract.
blocks.a: About 590 years earlier.

blocks.html: Thinking printing, paper and the compass were invented in Europe. They came from China first.

items: Make a stamp: draw a simple shape on a flat piece of craft foam or a potato half (a grown-up does any cutting), press it on an ink pad or in paint, and print it many times.
Write a letter on your stamp. Did it print backward? Printers in China carved their pages backward for this reason.

blocks.html: Going further. Ancient China earlier in this course: Ancient China. Find China and Japan in Countries of East Asia (World Geography).

blocks.html: In 1324, a king from West Africa set out to cross the Sahara on a pilgrimage to Mecca. Travelers said he brought thousands of people and camels carrying gold. When he stopped in Cairo, he gave away so much gold that its price fell there for years. He was Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, and people still call him one of the richest people who ever lived.

Africa was home to many great kingdoms. Aksum, in today's Ethiopia and Eritrea, traded across the Red Sea and became Christian in the 300s. Ghana and then Mali, in West Africa, grew rich from the trade of gold for salt across the Sahara. In southern Africa, the builders of Great Zimbabwe raised huge stone walls without mortar.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Some great kingdoms and cities of Africa.

blocks.html: Why trade gold for salt? In the south, near the gold fields, it was hot and people needed salt to stay healthy and to keep food from spoiling, but there was little salt there. In the Sahara there were great salt mines, but no gold. Camel caravans carried slabs of salt south and gold north.

Mali's city of Timbuktu became a center of learning, with scholars, mosques and libraries of handwritten books. Families there still keep thousands of old manuscripts on mathematics, astronomy, medicine and law.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: People of the kingdom of Mali.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: Kingdoms of Africa.

blocks.title: Trade
blocks.q: A caravan leaves the Sahara heading south. What is it most likely carrying to trade?
steps: The Sahara had salt mines but no gold.
The lands to the south had gold but little salt.
blocks.a: Salt, to trade for gold.

blocks.html: Thinking Africa had no great cities or kingdoms before Europeans arrived. Aksum, Mali, Great Zimbabwe and many others were rich and powerful long before.

items: Play a trading game: give one person "gold" (yellow paper squares) and another "salt" (white squares). Each needs some of the other's goods. Agree on a fair trade.
Find the Sahara, Mali and Ethiopia on a map or globe.

blocks.html: Going further. Africa's deserts, rivers and countries in Africa: Physical Features and Countries of West Africa. Africa's oldest kingdom is in Ancient Egypt for Young Explorers.

blocks.html: Deep in the rainforest of Central America, tall stone pyramids rise above the trees. Some are carved with rows of pictures and signs: the writing of the Maya. For a long time nobody could read it, but since the 1950s scholars have learned to read most of it, and now we know the names of Maya kings and the dates of their reigns.

In the Americas, three great civilizations built cities and empires: the Maya of Central America and southern Mexico (greatest about AD 250 to 900), the Aztecs of central Mexico (in the 1400s and early 1500s), and the Incas of the Andes mountains in South America (in the 1400s and early 1500s).

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Tikal (Maya), Tenochtitlan (Aztec), and Cusco and Machu Picchu (Inca).

head: Maya
Aztecs
Incas
rows: writing, a calendar, a symbol for zero
roads and rope bridges, knotted cords (quipu) for records

blocks.html: The Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in a lake. They built causeways to the shore and farmed on chinampas, garden beds built up in the shallow water. The Incas ruled an empire thousands of miles long, joined by about 25,000 miles of roads. Runners carried messages from station to station, and records were kept on knotted strings called quipu.

blocks.name: histstory-pic

items: Corn, beans and squash
Cacao (chocolate)
Llamas
Potatoes
Stone carvings

blocks.cap: Crops and animals of the Americas. Corn, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate all came from here.

blocks.html: In 1519, Spanish soldiers led by Hernán Cortés arrived in Mexico, and by 1521 the Aztec capital had fallen. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro began the conquest of the Incas. Sickness the Europeans carried, such as smallpox, which the people of the Americas had never met, killed far more people than the fighting did.

blocks.title: Maya numbers
blocks.q: The Maya wrote a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for zero. How would they write 13?
steps: That is two bars and three dots.
blocks.a: Two bars and three dots.

blocks.html: Thinking the Maya, Aztecs and Incas were one people at one time. They lived in different places, and the great Maya cities flourished centuries before the Aztec and Inca empires.

items: Write numbers the Maya way, with dots (1) and bars (5): try 7, 11 and 19. (Each level only goes up to 19.)
Look for foods from the Americas in your kitchen: corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, beans, squash, peanuts and chocolate.

blocks.html: Going further. The first peoples of North America in The First Peoples (Young Learners); for older students, Native Cultures in 1491 and The Spanish Empire (U.S. History I).

blocks.html: In about 1504, in the city of Florence, a young sculptor finished a statue carved from a single block of marble that other artists had given up on. It showed the shepherd boy David, about to face the giant Goliath, and it stood about 17 feet tall. The sculptor was Michelangelo, and he was not yet 30.

Renaissance means "rebirth." Beginning in the cities of Italy in the 1300s and 1400s, scholars studied old Greek and Latin books again, and artists studied the human body, light and perspective. Rich families like the Medici of Florence paid artists and scholars, and the new ideas spread across Europe.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Artists and scholars of the Renaissance.

blocks.html: Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519) painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He also filled thousands of notebook pages with drawings of birds in flight, flowing water, plants, the bones and muscles of the body, and ideas for machines, written in mirror writing from right to left. Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, lying on his back on high scaffolding, from 1508 to 1512.

Renaissance painters learned to use perspective: things far away are drawn smaller, and straight lines like the edges of a road meet at a point on the horizon. Their paintings looked deep, like windows.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: The Renaissance.

blocks.title: How old?
blocks.q: Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 and died in 1519. How old was he when he died?
steps: His birthday was in April and he died in May, so he had already turned 67.
blocks.a: 67 years old.

blocks.html: Thinking Leonardo was only a painter. He was also an engineer, an inventor and a scientist of nature.

items: Draw like Leonardo: sit by a window or in the yard and draw a plant, a bird or your own hand from life, looking carefully.
Draw a road going away from you: make its two edges meet at one point on the horizon. That is perspective.

blocks.html: Going further. The Art & Drawing Ladder teaches perspective and drawing from life. The young readers' path of Shakespeare: Romeo and Juliet meets the Renaissance in England.

Before 1450, almost every book in Europe was copied by hand. A Bible could take a scribe a year or more, so books were rare and costly. In the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg had an idea: what if each letter were a small piece of metal that could be set in rows, inked, printed, and then used again?

About 1450, Gutenberg built a printing press with movable metal type. Around 1455 he printed about 180 copies of the Bible. Within 50 years, presses in hundreds of towns had printed millions of books. Books became cheaper, more people learned to read, and new ideas spread faster than ever before.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Printing by machine and copying by hand.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: Printing and the Reformation.

blocks.html: In 1517, a monk and teacher named Martin Luther, in the town of Wittenberg, wrote 95 statements, the 95 Theses, arguing that some practices of the Church should change. Printers copied them, and within weeks they were read across Germany. This began the Reformation.

Western Christians divided. Those who followed reformers such as Luther and John Calvin came to be called Protestants. Those who stayed with the pope in Rome are Catholics; the Catholic Church also made reforms of its own at the Council of Trent. For more than a century, the two sides argued, and sometimes fought wars, over these beliefs. Today Catholics and Protestants live side by side in many countries.

blocks.title: Copies
blocks.q: A scribe copies one Bible in a year. A press prints about 180 Bibles in about three years. About how many Bibles does the press make in one year?
blocks.a: About 60, compared with the scribe's one.

blocks.html: Thinking Gutenberg invented printing. Printing with carved wooden blocks began in China, and movable type was used in China and Korea before him. Gutenberg's metal type and press worked fast and well for European alphabets.

items: Cut letters from a kitchen sponge or craft foam (with scissors). Glue them backward onto a piece of cardboard to spell a short word, dip in paint and print.
Why must the letters be backward? Look at a rubber stamp to check.

blocks.html: Going further. The young readers' paths of Erasmus: The Praise of Folly and Calvin: Institutes. Printing in China came first: Inventions of China.

Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean. His biggest ships were among the largest wooden ships ever built, and his fleets carried thousands of sailors to India, Arabia and the east coast of Africa. Then China's rulers ended the voyages and turned inward.

In the 1400s and 1500s, European sailors searched for sea routes to the spices and silks of Asia. Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa (1488). Christopher Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic and reached islands in the Caribbean (1492). Vasco da Gama reached India by sea (1498). Ferdinand Magellan's crew sailed all the way around the world (1519 to 1522).

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Three famous voyages: Columbus (1492), da Gama (1498) and Zheng He (1405 to 1433), roughly.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Explorers sought spices like pepper and cinnamon, which sold for high prices in Europe.

blocks.html: The voyages joined the two halves of the world. Plants, animals and people crossed the ocean in both directions: the Columbian Exchange. Europe, Africa and Asia got corn, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate; the Americas got horses, cattle, wheat and sugarcane. But Europeans also brought sicknesses such as smallpox, which killed a great many of the people of the Americas.

head: From the Americas
To the Americas
rows: diseases such as smallpox and measles

blocks.title: Around the world
blocks.q: Magellan's fleet left Spain in 1519 with five ships. One ship came home in 1522. Did Magellan himself finish the voyage?
steps: Magellan was killed in a battle in the Philippines in 1521.
Juan Sebastián Elcano led the last ship home.
blocks.a: No. His crew, led by Elcano, finished it.

blocks.html: Thinking Columbus proved the Earth was round. Educated people had known it was round since ancient Greek times. Columbus thought the Earth was smaller than it is and that Asia was close; he did not know the Americas were in the way.

items: On a globe, use a piece of string to trace Columbus's route from Spain to the Caribbean, and da Gama's from Portugal around Africa to India. Which is longer?
Find three foods in your kitchen that came from the Americas, and three that came to the Americas.

blocks.html: Going further. Explorers (Young Learners); for older students, European Exploration and The Columbian Exchange (U.S. History I). Map skills in Latitude.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: For more than 1,000 years, most people believed the Earth sat still at the center of everything, with the Sun, Moon and stars circling around it. It certainly looks that way. In 1543, a Polish astronomer named Nicolaus Copernicus published a book that said the opposite: the Earth spins, and it travels around the Sun.

In the Scientific Revolution (about 1543 to 1700), people began to test ideas with careful observations, measurements and experiments, and to describe nature with mathematics. Copernicus put the Sun at the center; Galileo turned a telescope to the sky; Isaac Newton explained gravity and motion.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Three scientists of the Scientific Revolution.

blocks.html: In 1609 and 1610, Galileo Galilei built telescopes and looked at the night sky. He saw mountains on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way, and four moons circling Jupiter. Those moons showed that not everything circles the Earth. Galileo's ideas brought him into a long conflict with Church authorities, who put him on trial in 1633.

In 1687, Isaac Newton showed that the same force, gravity, makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon going around the Earth. His laws of motion still help engineers build bridges and send spacecraft to other planets.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline

events: Copernicus: the Earth goes around the Sun
Newton's laws of motion and gravity

blocks.cap: The Scientific Revolution.

blocks.title: Test it
blocks.q: An old idea said heavy things fall faster than light things. How could you test it?
steps: Drop two balls of the same size but different weights from the same height at the same time.
Listen for them to hit the ground. (They land together, unless air slows one a lot.)
blocks.a: With an experiment: drop them together and watch.

blocks.html: Thinking Galileo invented the telescope. Spectacle makers in the Netherlands made the first ones in 1608; Galileo made better ones and used them to study the sky.

items: On a clear night, look at the Moon with binoculars. Can you see mountains and craters, as Galileo did? (Never look at the Sun.)
Drop a heavy ball and a light ball of the same size together from the same height. Which lands first?

blocks.html: Going further. The young readers' paths of Copernicus: On the Revolutions, Galileo: Two New Sciences and Newton: Principia. Explore the Night Sky in the Science Lab, and science for ages 9 and 10 in Science Explorers.

On July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia, leaders from thirteen British colonies in North America approved a declaration. It said that "all men are created equal" and have rights to "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness," and that the colonies were now free and independent states. This was the Declaration of Independence, written mostly by Thomas Jefferson.

The colonists had protested British taxes passed without their votes: "no taxation without representation." Fighting began in 1775. Led by George Washington and helped by France, the Americans won the Revolutionary War, and Britain recognized their independence in 1783. In 1787 they wrote the Constitution, and in 1789 Washington became the first president.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: The colonies were across the Atlantic Ocean from Britain, more than 3,000 miles away.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Not every colonist wanted independence: Patriots did, Loyalists stayed loyal to the king.

blocks.html: Americans were divided. Patriots wanted independence; Loyalists wanted to stay British; many people just hoped to stay out of the fighting. Enslaved people and American Indian nations made hard choices too, and some fought on each side, hoping for freedom or to keep their lands.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline

events: Fighting begins at Lexington and Concord
Treaty of Paris: the war ends

blocks.cap: The American Revolution.

blocks.title: How long was the war?
blocks.q: The fighting began in 1775, and the peace treaty was signed in 1783. About how long did the war last?
blocks.a: About eight years.

blocks.html: Thinking the war ended when the Declaration was signed in 1776. Declaring independence was one thing; winning it took until 1783.

items: Read the opening of the Declaration of Independence aloud, from "We hold these truths to be self-evident."
Write a family "declaration": three rights you think everyone in your home should have, and three duties that go with them.

blocks.html: Going further. In Young Learners: The Declaration of Independence and George Washington. In U.S. History I: The Declaration of Independence and The Revolutionary War. The young readers' path of American State Papers.

sources.name: Natural Earth (public domain map data), simplified for the map

blocks.html: On July 14, 1789, crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille, an old fortress-prison that stood for the king's power. France had a king with almost unlimited power, nobles and clergy who paid few taxes, and ordinary people who paid most of them while bread grew very expensive. Today the French celebrate July 14 as their national holiday.

In the French Revolution, which began in 1789, the people of France ended the king's absolute rule. Their motto was "Liberty, equality, fraternity" (brotherhood). They wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which said that people are born free and equal in rights. In 1792 France became a republic.

The revolution also brought fear and war. In 1793 King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette were executed, and in the Reign of Terror that followed, thousands of people accused of being enemies of the revolution were put to death. Wars with the kings of Europe went on for years.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: A king, a worker of Paris and a general.

blocks.html: A young general named Napoleon Bonaparte won battle after battle. In 1799 he took power, and in 1804 he crowned himself emperor. His law code, the Napoleonic Code, spread ideas such as equality before the law across Europe. But his armies were finally beaten at Waterloo, in today's Belgium, in 1815.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Napoleon's wars reached from Spain to Moscow. In 1812 his army marched to Moscow and back through a terrible winter.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline
blocks.cap: The French Revolution and Napoleon.

blocks.title: Compare
blocks.q: The American Declaration of Independence was in 1776; the French Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1789. Which came first, and by how many years?
blocks.a: The American Declaration, by 13 years. Some French leaders, like Lafayette, had fought in the American war.

blocks.html: Thinking Napoleon was very short. He was about average height for a Frenchman of his time; the story comes partly from a mix-up between French and English inches, and partly from cartoons drawn by his enemies.

items: Talk it over at dinner: what do liberty, equality and fraternity mean in your own family or school? Can you have all three at once?
Find France, Belgium and Russia on a map. How far did Napoleon's army march to Moscow?

blocks.html: Going further. The young readers' paths of Rousseau: The Social Contract and Tolstoy: War and Peace (Napoleon in Russia). Europe's countries in Countries of Western Europe.

sources.name: Grokipedia, "Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen"

blocks.html: In 1750, almost all cloth in Britain was spun and woven by hand, at home. A family might spin thread all winter. By 1850, huge mills full of whirring machines made more cloth in a day than a whole village could make in a year. Something big had changed.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 1700s. Machines driven by water wheels and then by steam engines began to do work that people had done by hand. Work moved from homes into factories, people moved from farms to cities, and railways carried goods and people faster than ever.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: An inventor, a factory worker and a farmer.

blocks.html: Steam engines burned coal to boil water; the steam pushed a piston back and forth. Thomas Newcomen built engines to pump water out of mines in 1712, and James Watt made a far better, more efficient one in the 1770s. In 1830, the first railway between two big cities, Liverpool and Manchester, opened, with steam locomotives like George Stephenson's Rocket.

Factories made goods cheaper, and over time many families became better off. But early factory work was hard and dangerous. Workers, including young children, often worked 12 or more hours a day, and city streets were crowded and dirty. Reformers pushed for change: in 1833 Britain's Factory Act limited children's working hours, and later laws required children to go to school.

blocks.title: Faster
blocks.q: A hand spinner makes 1 spool of thread a day. A mill machine run by one worker makes 50 spools a day. How many hand spinners would it take to keep up?
blocks.a: 50 hand spinners.

blocks.html: Thinking James Watt invented the steam engine. Earlier engines, like Newcomen's, already pumped water from mines. Watt's engine used much less coal, which made steam power worth using almost everywhere.

items: Hold a race: one person makes five paper cards alone (fold, draw a star, write a name). Then a team of three makes five, each person doing one step, like a factory line. Which is faster? Which is more fun?
Look around your home: what was made in a factory? Is anything handmade?

blocks.html: Going further. Inventors (Young Learners), and The Market Revolution and Industrialization for older students. The young readers' path of Adam Smith: The Wealth of Nations starts with a pin factory. Energy and machines in Energy Changes Form (Science Explorers).

In 1789, a man named Olaudah Equiano published the story of his life. He wrote that as a boy he had been kidnapped in West Africa, carried across the Atlantic in a crowded slave ship and sold. He later bought his own freedom. His book was read all over Britain and helped turn many people against the slave trade.

Slavery, owning people as property and forcing them to work, existed in many places since ancient times. From the 1500s to the 1800s, about 12 million Africans were carried across the Atlantic and enslaved in the Americas. In the late 1700s, a movement called abolition began to fight to end it.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Four people who fought slavery. (Drawn as cartoons, not likenesses.)

blocks.html: In Britain, William Wilberforce spoke against the slave trade in Parliament year after year. In 1807 Britain banned the slave trade, and from 1834 slavery ended in most of the British Empire. In the United States, Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became a great speaker and writer for freedom. Harriet Tubman escaped too, then went back again and again to lead others north to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

In the United States, the question of slavery helped lead to the Civil War (1861 to 1865). President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863, and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in the whole country in 1865. Brazil, the last country in the Americas, ended slavery in 1888.

blocks.name: histstory-timeline

events: Slavery ends in most of the British Empire

blocks.cap: The long fight to end slavery.

blocks.title: How long a fight?
blocks.q: Britain banned its slave trade in 1807. Brazil ended slavery in 1888. How many years apart?
blocks.a: 81 years. Ending slavery took a long time and great courage.

blocks.html: Thinking slavery ended everywhere at the same time. Each country ended it in its own year, after long struggles.

items: On a clear night, find the Big Dipper. The two stars at the end of its cup point to the North Star. People escaping slavery followed it north.
Read a few sentences from Frederick Douglass's writings together, and talk about why he thought reading was the "pathway from slavery to freedom."

blocks.html: Going further. Slavery and Freedom and Heroes of Freedom (Young Learners); Abolition and Emancipation (U.S. History I).

blocks.html: On December 17, 1903, on a windy beach at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, a homemade airplane rolled along a wooden rail and lifted into the air. It flew for 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Its builders, the brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright, owned a bicycle shop. Before the day was over, they had flown four times; the longest flight lasted 59 seconds.

The 1800s and early 1900s were an age of invention. In about 70 years, the world got the telegraph (Samuel Morse, 1844), the telephone (Alexander Graham Bell, 1876), a practical electric light (Thomas Edison, 1879), the automobile (Karl Benz, 1886) and the airplane (the Wright brothers, 1903).

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Inventors and scientists of the age of invention.

blocks.html: Marie Curie, born in Poland, studied in Paris, where women were rarely allowed to be scientists. With her husband Pierre, she discovered two new elements, polonium and radium. She won the Nobel Prize twice, in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911), the first person ever to win two.

blocks.title: How fast was it?
blocks.q: The Wrights' first flight covered 120 feet in 12 seconds. How many feet did it travel each second?
blocks.a: 10 feet each second, about as fast as a person running.

blocks.html: Thinking Edison invented the light bulb all alone. Others made glowing lamps before him. Edison and his team made a bulb that lasted a long time, and built power stations to bring electricity to homes.

items: Fold three paper airplanes of different shapes. Fly each three times from the same spot and measure the distance. Which design flies farthest? (That is a fair test, like the Wrights' experiments.)
Ask a grandparent which inventions came into your family's home in their lifetime.

blocks.html: Going further. Inventors (Young Learners). Circuits and light bulbs in Circuits (Science Explorers). Fly a rocket in the Rocket lab.

Every year on November 11, many countries keep a moment of silence. It marks the hour in 1918 when the guns stopped at the end of World War I: the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. Americans call it Veterans Day, and many other countries call it Remembrance Day.

In the 1900s, two terrible wars were fought by many nations around the world. World War I (1914 to 1918) was fought mostly in Europe, between the Allies (including Britain, France, Russia and, from 1917, the United States) and the Central Powers (including Germany and Austria-Hungary). World War II (1939 to 1945) was even bigger.
In World War I, soldiers dug long lines of trenches and fought for years over small pieces of land. About 9 million soldiers died. The war ended with the armistice of November 11, 1918.

In the 1930s, Adolf Hitler and his Nazi party took power in Germany. In 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war. Germany, Italy and Japan fought the Allies: Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States (from 1941, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor), China and many others. On D-Day, June 6, 1944, Allied soldiers landed on the beaches of France. Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August 1945.

During the war the Nazis carried out the Holocaust: they murdered about six million Jewish men, women and children, and millions of other people. Many brave people risked their lives to hide and rescue those in danger. We remember, so that it never happens again.

blocks.cap: Two world wars.

blocks.name: histstory-map
blocks.cap: Capitals of some of the nations in the world wars.

blocks.html: After the war, in 1945, countries formed the United Nations, a place where nations could talk out their disagreements and work together to keep the peace.

blocks.title: Between the wars
blocks.q: World War I ended in 1918. World War II began in 1939. How many years of peace were there between them?
blocks.a: 21 years.

blocks.html: Mixing up the two wars. World War I came first (1914 to 1918); World War II came later (1939 to 1945).

items: On November 11, keep a moment of silence with your family at 11 o'clock.
Ask an older relative whether anyone in your family served in either war, and what they remember hearing about it.

blocks.html: On July 20, 1969, about 600 million people watched on black-and-white television as astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped from his spacecraft onto the Moon. "That's one small step for man," he said, "one giant leap for mankind." Buzz Aldrin joined him a few minutes later.

After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals in a long Cold War (about 1947 to 1991). They never fought each other directly; they competed with weapons, spies, allies and a space race. The Soviet Union launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in 1957 and the first person into space, Yuri Gagarin, in 1961; Americans landed on the Moon in 1969.

blocks.name: histstory-person
blocks.cap: Space travel and computers changed the world in the late 1900s.

blocks.html: Germany's capital, Berlin, was split in two, and in 1961 a wall was built across the city. On November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened, and people climbed on it and chipped it apart. Germany was reunited in 1990, and in 1991 the Soviet Union broke up into 15 countries. The Cold War was over.

Meanwhile, the civil rights movement in the United States, led by people like Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., worked to end unfair laws that kept Black Americans apart and unequal. New nations in Africa and Asia won their independence. Computers grew from room-sized machines to desktops, and in 1989 to 1991 Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web.

blocks.title: How long?
blocks.q: Sputnik went up in 1957. Astronauts walked on the Moon in 1969. How many years after the first satellite was the first Moon landing?
blocks.a: Only 12 years.

blocks.html: Thinking the Cold War was full of battles between the United States and the Soviet Union. The two never fought each other directly, though wars were fought elsewhere, such as in Korea and Vietnam.

items: Interview a parent or grandparent: What was the first computer or phone you used? What did you do before the internet?
Make a family technology time line: when did your family first get a TV, a computer, a cell phone?
